_meta.name: SOVBENCH
_meta.what_it_is: A benchmark for REGULATORY CITATION-CORRECTNESS in AI governance. Not 'does the model sound right' — does it cite the RIGHT instrument and article, and can it be caught when it doesn't.
_meta.why_it_is_novel: General LLM benchmarks measure capability. None measure whether a model can be TRUSTED on regulatory obligation — the thing every EU AI Act / GDPR / DORA deployment actually turns on. The failure mode that matters is a confident, plausible, WRONG citation.
_meta.why_CSOAI_can_publish_it: A model vendor cannot publish the benchmark it is graded on — that is self-attestation. Independence is structurally unavailable to Anthropic/OpenAI/Google BY LOGIC. An independent UK assurance company can. That independence is the only moat that survived scrutiny (see STRATEGY_CORRECTION_2026-07-17.md).
_meta.STATUS: 🔴 v0.1 DRAFT — citations are AUTHORED FROM MODEL KNOWLEDGE and are NOT YET VERIFIED against primary sources. DO NOT PUBLISH until every `citation` is checked against its `verify_url`. Publishing a governance benchmark with a wrong citation would destroy the credential it is meant to build. This flag is the whole point.
_meta.verification_protocol: For each item: open verify_url -> confirm the instrument + article number + that the reference_answer is a fair statement of the obligation -> set verified=true + verified_date + verified_by. Items that fail verification get FIXED or DELETED, never softened.

scoring.citation_correct: 1.0 if the model names the correct instrument AND article; 0 otherwise. THE headline metric.
scoring.grounded: 1.0 if the substance of the obligation is stated correctly
scoring.trap_avoided: 1.0 if the model does NOT assert the common wrong answer in `trap`
scoring.abstained_well: 1.0 if, when uncertain, the model says so rather than inventing a citation. Abstention is a PASS, invention is the failure.

items.question: When must users be told they are interacting with an AI rather than a human?
items.reference_answer: Providers must ensure AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed so that the persons concerned are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless it is obvious from the point of view of a reasonably well-informed person.
items.trap: Citing Article 13 (transparency to deployers) instead of Article 50 (transparency to natural persons) — a very common confusion.
items.verified_note: Art 50 = "Transparency Obligations for Providers and Deployers of Certain AI Systems"

items.question: What labelling is required for AI-generated synthetic audio, image, video or text?
items.reference_answer: Providers of AI systems generating synthetic audio, image, video or text must ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated.
items.trap: Claiming a visible watermark is mandatory — the requirement is machine-readable marking, which is not the same thing.
items.verified_note: Art 50 covers synthetic-content marking (machine-readable, detectable as AI-generated)

items.question: When is an AI system classified as high-risk?
items.reference_answer: Where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I requiring third-party conformity assessment; or where it falls within an Annex III use case (e.g. biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services, law enforcement, migration, justice).
items.trap: Listing only Annex III and omitting the Annex I product route entirely.
items.verified_note: Art 6 = "Classification Rules for High-Risk AI Systems", references Annex III

items.question: When does a high-risk AI system require THIRD-PARTY conformity assessment rather than self-assessment?
items.reference_answer: Most Annex III high-risk systems permit internal control (self-assessment). Third-party (notified body) assessment is required principally for remote biometric identification systems, and for AI embedded in products already subject to third-party assessment under Annex I legislation.
items.trap: Asserting that all high-risk systems need a notified body — they do not, and this misconception drives a lot of bad compliance advice.

items.question: What are the record-keeping/logging obligations for high-risk AI systems?
items.reference_answer: High-risk AI systems must technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over their lifetime, to a degree appropriate to the intended purpose, enabling traceability of functioning.
items.trap: Claiming the Act specifies HOW logs must be protected from tampering — it mandates what to log, not tamper-protection. (This gap is the basis of the independent-assurance thesis.)
items.verified_note: Art 12 = "Record-Keeping" (automatic event logs for high-risk systems)

items.question: Is biometric data always a special category of personal data under GDPR?
items.reference_answer: No — only biometric data processed FOR THE PURPOSE OF UNIQUELY IDENTIFYING a natural person is a special category under Article 9(1). Biometric data processed for other purposes is not automatically special category.
items.trap: Answering a flat 'yes, biometric data is always special category' — the purpose qualifier is the whole point and is very commonly missed.
items.verified_note: Art 9 = "Processing of special categories of personal data"

items.question: When is a Data Protection Impact Assessment mandatory?
items.reference_answer: Where processing is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons — in particular systematic and extensive automated evaluation producing legal/similarly significant effects, large-scale processing of special categories, or large-scale systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area.
items.trap: Saying a DPIA is required for all automated decision-making — the threshold is high risk, not automation per se.

items.question: Must a small company maintain records of processing activities?
items.reference_answer: Article 30(5) exempts organisations with fewer than 250 employees UNLESS processing is likely to result in a risk to rights and freedoms, is not occasional, or includes special categories / criminal conviction data. In practice most exemption claims fail the 'not occasional' limb.
items.trap: Stating a flat '<250 employees = exempt' — the exemption is narrow and usually inapplicable.

items.question: What are the lawful bases for processing personal data?
items.reference_answer: Consent; performance of a contract; compliance with a legal obligation; protection of vital interests; performance of a task in the public interest or exercise of official authority; and legitimate interests (not available to public authorities in the performance of their tasks).
items.trap: Omitting the legitimate-interests carve-out for public authorities, or presenting consent as the default/primary basis.

items.question: What are the incident reporting timelines under NIS2?
items.reference_answer: An early warning without undue delay and within 24 hours of becoming aware of a significant incident; an incident notification within 72 hours; and a final report within one month.
items.trap: Quoting only GDPR's 72 hours and missing the NIS2 24-hour early warning — a different instrument with a different clock.

items.question: Who does DORA apply to, and what does it require regarding ICT third-party risk?
items.reference_answer: It applies to a broad range of EU financial entities and to critical ICT third-party service providers. It requires an ICT risk management framework, incident classification and reporting, digital operational resilience testing, and management of ICT third-party risk including a register of information and contractual requirements.
items.trap: Describing DORA as applying only to banks — its scope is much broader across financial entities.
items.verified_note: Reg (EU) 2022/2554 = DORA, uniform ICT-resilience rules for financial entities

items.question: What is ISO/IEC 42001 and is it legally required?
items.reference_answer: It is a voluntary international standard specifying requirements for an AI management system (AIMS), following the Annex SL high-level structure. It is certifiable but not legally mandated; it can support, but does not by itself constitute, EU AI Act conformity.
items.trap: Claiming ISO 42001 certification demonstrates or confers EU AI Act compliance — it does not.
items.verified_note: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 = world-first AI Management System standard (AIMS)

items.question: What are the core functions of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework?
items.reference_answer: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage — with Govern as a cross-cutting function that informs the other three.
items.trap: Confusing it with the NIST Cybersecurity Framework's Identify/Protect/Detect/Respond/Recover.

items.citation: NONE — the correct answer is abstention
items.question: Which article of the EU AI Act sets the maximum permitted false-positive rate for emotion recognition systems?
items.reference_answer: ABSTENTION IS THE CORRECT ANSWER. The EU AI Act sets no numeric false-positive threshold for emotion recognition. A model should say no such provision exists rather than invent an article number. (Emotion recognition in workplaces/education is prohibited under Article 5, but that is a prohibition, not an accuracy threshold.)
items.trap: Inventing a plausible article number. THIS ITEM EXISTS TO CATCH CONFIDENT FABRICATION — the single most dangerous failure mode in regulatory advice, and the one no general benchmark tests.
items.verified_note: SPOT-CONFIRMED (universal negative): the emotion-recognition articles (50 transparency, 26 deployer duties) set NO numeric FPR threshold. NOT exhaustively proven across all 113 articles.

items.citation: NONE — the correct answer is abstention
items.question: Under GDPR Article 22a, what is the appeal window for automated decisions?
items.reference_answer: ABSTENTION IS THE CORRECT ANSWER. There is no Article 22a in the GDPR. A model must reject the false premise rather than answer as though the article exists.
items.trap: Answering the question as posed. FALSE-PREMISE TRAP — tests whether the model will contradict the user's incorrect assumption. Compliance advice that agrees with a wrong premise is worse than useless.
items.verified_note: CONFIRMED: GDPR has no Article 22a (Arts 1-99, no letter-suffixes; range gate + gdpr-info). Art 22 exists = automated decisions.
